content:Speaker assistant says: 1. Nutrient variety: Plan to include a variety of nutrients in your meals, including carbohydrates, proteins, healthy fats, vitamins and minerals.

2. Portion control: Limit your intake of high-calorie foods and ensure you are consuming appropriate portions consistently.

3. Whole foods: Incorporate whole foods such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean protein sources, and healthy fats in your diet.

4. Hydration: Drink sufficient water and avoid high-calorie beverages.

5. Meal planning: Planning your meals ahead of time is an excellent way to ensure you consume a balanced and healthy diet.

6. Mindful eating: Practice mindful eating and pay attention to your body's signals of being hungry or full.

7. Exercise: Incorporating regular exercise into your routine helps you maintain a healthy weight and allows the body to utilize nutrients more efficiently.

To ensure you stick to your healthy and balanced diet, here are some tips:

1. Make gradual changes: Changing your diet drastically can be challenging. Instead, make gradual changes one step at a time.

2. Keep track of your progress: Tracking your progress can help keep you motivated and understand the benefits of healthy eating over time.

3. Stay focused: Focus on the benefits of healthy eating, such as improved energy, mood, and fewer health issues later on.

4. Celebrate your successes: Celebrate your milestones, no matter how small. It will help you stay motivated and maintain your healthy diet.

5. Find a support system: Connect with family, friends, or professionals who share your health goals or invest in a fitness app.

6. Don't give up: Nutrition is a lifelong journey, and there will always be setbacks. content:Speaker user says: I struggle with eating healthy when I am out with friends or at social events. What tips do you have for sticking to a healthy diet in these situations? context:social events keywords: eating, health, social situations, diet tags: eating, portion control

content:Speaker assistant says: Here are some tips for sticking to a healthy diet when you're out with friends or at social events:

1. Plan ahead: Check out the menu or food options before you go and decide what healthy options you can choose. You can also eat before you go, so you're not as hungry, and less likely to be tempted by unhealthy options.

2. Be mindful: Pay attention to the food you're eating, savor each bite, and avoid distractions like your phone. This will help you eat more slowly and make better choices.

3. Choose wisely: Stick to vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and healthy fats. Avoid fried or processed foods, creamy sauces, and sugary drinks.

4. Be assertive: Don't be afraid to ask for substitutions or make special requests to ensure your food is prepared in a healthier way.

5. Control portions: Keep portions in check by sharing a meal with a friend, ordering a smaller size option, or taking leftovers home.

6. Stay hydrated: Drink water or unsweetened drinks instead of alcohol and sugary drinks.

7. Bring a healthy dish: If possible, offer to bring a healthy dish or snack to share with others.

content:Speaker user says: Make sure your between-meals nibbles boost your nutritional bottom line.
It's 4-o'clock in the afternoon, lunch is a distant memory, and dinner is still a long way off. Do you fall for the siren song of the break room vending machine or tuck into a light, healthful snack? Either way, if you eat between meals, you're part of a bigger trend. Snacking has become the new normal, and according to market research firm Hartman Group, half of the times we eat revolve around snacks, from early-morning nibbles to late-night noshes.
That's just fine, says Cheryl Forberg, RD, nutritionist on The Biggest Loser and author of A Small Guide to Losing Big—as long as you're smart about it. In fact, you should eat snacks, especially if you're trying to lose weight. "A lot of people skip snacks, thinking it's smart weight-loss strategy, and that's a big mistake," she says. "They're just stunned you're telling them to eat more often." In reality, healthful, satisfying bites regulate your appetite, preventing overeating and boosting the overall quality of your diet.
But for many of us, snacks are so incidental that we tend to overlook them—and the calories they add to our daily tally. In a recent study in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, volunteers wore cameras to compare what they recalled eating with what they actually ate. Their most underreported item: afternoon snacks.
In addition to being mindful of how snacks may contribute to your daily calorie intake, make sure you're not falling for faux-healthy ones. Trail mix, dried fruit, and flavored fat-free yogurt are three that seem virtuous but can be sugar bombs, says fitness trainer Dalton Wong, author of The Feelgood Plan: Happier, Healthier & Slimmer in 15 Minutes a Day. Packaged snacks may be convenient, but their saturated fat, sugar, and sodium can pile up fast. Keep a close eye on Nutrition Facts labels and ingredient lists, and choose snacks that offer a satisfying mix of protein, complex carbohydrates, and good-for-you fats. Follow these trips to make sure your choices between meals help, instead of harm, your diet.
Schedule snacks just as you do meals, Forberg says, so you know what you'll eat and when. She even recommends adding snacks in your calendar so you won't forget. "Once you get into the habit and start doing that, you're going to notice the difference in your energy, and it will change your hunger cues," Forberg says. "You're not going to be as hungry at your next meal, and you won't need as much food to feel full."
Given our grazing ways, it's easy to load up on snacks that are really meals. "Calorie-wise, a snack is half the calories of a meal," Forberg says. Whatever your caloric needs might be, Cooking Light's guidelines recommend keeping snacks below 200 calories, 10g sugar, and 250mg of sodium, and aiming for at least 5g of protein per serving. If it's a starchy-snack, make sure it's a whole grain and has at least 3g of fiber.
Just like meals, snacks should be a satisfying combination of protein, healthy fats, and complex carbs. "A lot of people assume that an apple is a great snack. And it is," Forberg says. "But if you're just having fruit, what happens is you get the energy, your blood sugar goes up, and then it drops down and you're hungry and tired again." Add a little protein to the mix, such as a mozzarella cheese stick or a handful of nuts, she says, "and your blood sugar goes up slowly and stays steady longer so your energy is sustained, your satiety is sustained, and your blood sugar is in a healthier place." Good fats also help keep blood sugar in balance, Wong says: "If you want something sweet like chocolate, then have it with some nuts. Having something sweet coupled with a healthy fat will lower the rate of how your body uses the sugar so you don't get a sugar rush or crash."
Having a hard time resisting the chips in the break room or the candy on your coworker's desk? Poor sleep may be to blame. In a recent study in the journal Sleep, volunteers who had their sleep restricted for four nights, reported more hunger and had a harder time resisting junky snacks than those who got adequate rest. "A good night's sleep will allow you to make better food choices throughout the day and avoid that craving for junk food," Wong says. So to snack smarter, make sure to get your z's. How can adding a little protein to a fruit snack help sustain energy and satiety levels? context:memory 181 keywords: snacking, nutrition, appetite, calories, snacks, Hartman Group, Cheryl Forberg, Dalton Wong, sleep, satiety, protein tags: snack, healthy, preparation

content:Speaker assistant says: Of course! Here are some tips on how to read Nutrition Facts labels so you can make informed decisions when choosing snacks:

1. Look at serving size: The serving size on the label should be your starting point when evaluating a snack. Make sure to adjust the rest of the information to match your portion size.

2. Check calories: The total calories per serving should be noted, and it’s important to factor that in when deciding how much of the snack to eat.

3. Pay attention to fats: Aim for snacks that have low amounts of saturated and trans fats, the “bad” fats that can harm heart health. Instead, opt for snacks that have high amounts of unsaturated fats, which are healthier.

4. Look at sugar content: Many packaged snacks have a high sugar content, including those marketed as “healthy.” Try to choose snacks that have less than 10 grams of sugar per serving, and avoid those that list sugar as the first ingredient.

5. Review sodium levels: Excessive sodium can lead to high blood pressure, so it’s important to keep an eye on how much you consume. Look for snacks that have less than 250 milligrams of sodium per serving.

6. Check the ingredients: Look for snacks that have whole foods as their main ingredients, such as whole grains, fruits, and vegetables. Avoid products with long lists of ingredients or that contain added preservatives and artificial flavors.

By following these tips, you can make sure that the snacks you choose are nutritious and aligned with your dietary goals. context:This document provides guidance on reading Nutrition Facts labels to help individuals make informed choices when selecting snacks. 3. Take Breaks: Take short breaks every 45-50 minutes to avoid burnout and to recharge your mind.

4. Use Study Tools: Use study tools that can help you stay organized and on track, such as flashcards or study guides.

5. Choose the Right Study Environment: Find an environment that suits your studying preferences, whether it's complete silence or some background noise.

7. Stay Motivated: Keep reminding yourself of your goals, congratulate yourself after completing important tasks and reward yourself after achieving your goals.
